speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the last 20 minutes I have listened with a great deal of interest indeed to the remarks of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) because, coming from the Pacific coast and representing a Pacific coast riding, I am aware, as he is, of the great importance of the inland waterway which serves the province of British Columbia, a considerable portion of the state of Washington, and stretches northward to the southern borders of Alaska. You may start below Seattle and sail northward for 1,000 miles on an inland waterway which comes upon the open sea only once for a brief time in that whole passage.
This great waterway is full of marine traffic to the extent that you are hardly ever during the whole voyage out of sight of another vessel of some kind ploughing up and down these inland passages. Moreover, this traffic not only covers the coast line itself, but the indented fiords along the coast, running many miles inland, reaching lumber camps, pulp and paper mills, fish canneries, Indian villages, and other settlements steadily growing and increasing in importance up and down the coast of British Columbia. This is a scene of which my hon. friend is well aware, and he, like myself and other members from British Columbia, is well aware how important is the domestic traffic on these great inland waterways to the people of British Columbia and to much of its commerce.
To give the house some idea of the extent of the traffic which moves along inland waterways, I should like to refer to a supplement to the 1963 annual report of the national harbours board which contains some interesting figures on this question. Turning to the figures for the port of Vancouver, the total domestic cargo tonnage for 1959-I am eliminating foreign cargo tonnage because we are discussing in this bill inland traffic, not overseas traffic-was 4,900,000 tons, or in round figures 5 million tons. In 1963 it had increased 2 million tons to a figure of approximately 7 million tons. That is the total inward and outward domestic tonnage.
If I may compare that 7 million tons of domestic traffic with the traffic in and out of the port of Montreal, in 1959 the figure was 7,700,000 tons approximately, and by 1963

it had moved up to 9,300,000 tons. Therefore the domestic traffic in and out of Vancouver compares very favourably, with a ratio of approximately seven to nine, with the port of Montreal, which gives some indication to the house of the extensive traffic which plies our inland coastal waters.
I want to turn for a moment to the figures for the port of Vancouver for passenger traffic, because my hon. friend mentioned them when discussing the shift in coastal traffic by vessels in the inland waters. I refer to these figures because this is a matter of considerable importance in plotting how traffic should be governed in the future under legislation such as that suggested by my hon. friend today.
In 1959 coast wise traffic in total numbers of passengers, again excluding foreign traffic, taking both landings and embarkations into consideration, amounted to 1,000,183. This number declined steadily until in 1963-and this figure is hardly believable-the number of passengers was down to 198,000. Some of that drop from 1,000,183 to 198,000 had to do with some changes in ferry service and the withdrawal of some of the old ferry services between Vancouver, Nanaimo and Victoria. But, as my hon. friend conceded, there has been a very marked decline indeed in coast wise passenger movements.
There has also been a comparable change in the number of vessel movements, and I want to refer to this for a moment because it is quite significant. I am sorry I have no comparative figures here, but coastal or inland commercial vessels, including fishery vessels, numbered 22,316 in 1962 and 19,325 in 1963. This is in terms of arrivals only. These figures give, I believe, some indication of the importance of this traffic.
In listening to the hon. gentleman's remarks I wondered whether or not it was wise to attempt further to regulate this traffic through a federal agency and to remove the regulation of that traffic from the area of provincial jurisdiction in which for the most part it now rests. It is this point to which I wish to come next. As this question is peculiar to British Columbia and has to do to some extent with the growth and direct development of British Columbia, I wonder whether or not we are wise in bringing this domestic traffic into the federal field in the manner suggested by my hon. friend.

speechtext: I think this is quite true. This traffic is literally self-regulating today in the province of British Columbia. I might explain, although I am sure my hon. friend knows this, that the movement of ships, for instance, for use at pulp mills up and down the coast and for the movement of paper from the pulp mills down the coast to Vancouver and further to Seattle is done in two ways. Contracts are let for this movement at the beginning of the season. The job is put out to tender and the various barge operators on the coast contract with the operators of the mills or the shippers for the hauling of the paper and chips from the mills.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PUBLIC CARRIERS IN B.C. COASTAL WATERS
speechtext: Is not the hon. member aware that my bill refers only to the public carriage of goods and passengers? It has no relationship to the contract carriage of bulk goods.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PUBLIC CARRIERS IN B.C. COASTAL WATERS
speechtext:
I am sure that the barges operated by commercial barging companies are classified as commercial carriers; that these carriers who contract for the movement of goods are in fact the carriers of the goods for the shipping company, and would thereby be classed as public carriers. I see my hon. friend shaking his head, but I do not know just how I could classify them. If a barge company, for example, is not in the special business of hauling pulp and paper, but is in a commercial business, then I believe that company would be classified as a public carrier. I believe it is a public carrier whether its goods are moved under a tariff or whether its goods are carried under contract.
I should like to go on and point out some of the features relating to the exemptions under section 12 of the Transport Act to which my hon. friend referred, and which I feel he rather skipped over. I do not want to leave this section without explaining it a little more fully. This is the one that deals with exemptions under the act. I quote from section 12, subsection 4:
The provisions of this part do not apply in the case of ships engaged in the transport of goods or passengers,
(a)	between ports or places in British Columbia-
It was there that my hon. friend stopped
early in his remarks. However, the section continues as follows:
(b)	between ports or places in Hudson bay, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland, and the gulf and river St. Lawrence east of the western point of the island of Orleans, or between any two or more places therein, nor does this part apply between any of such ports or places and ports or places outside of Canada.
Thus the exemptions which my hon. friend mentioned in explaining the act apply to the

Transport Act
west coast, to Hudson bay, to the east coast of Canada and to the lower reaches of the St. Lawrence river. In other words, what we are looking at here is not a section of the act in respect of the control of shipping which relates to seaborne craft at all. The section is specifically designed to cover lake vessels and the upper St. Lawrence reaches and in no way at all relates to traffic on the west coast, the east coast or in any of the salt waters surrounding Canada. I think this should be made perfectly clear as we consider this act which specifically relates to traffic on the great lakes, on the upper St. Lawrence regions and in no way relates to traffic on the British Columbia coast.
I want to move on a little bit to consider for a moment the changing nature of services on the west coast. My friend will remember that his area was at one time served by the old Princess Alberni, which called at his port and at other ports up the coast along the west coast of Vancouver island. A number of years ago this old vessel was suspended from service, I believe, and is probably running guns into Cyprus today or performing some other useful task. It is also true that about the time when this service was suspended a road was driven through from Port Alberni and people can now, for the first time go through to the Pacific ocean, even if they are not going on some business for the McMillan, Bloedel Company.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PUBLIC CARRIERS IN B.C. COASTAL WATERS
speechtext: Only if you are going at night or on week ends.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PUBLIC CARRIERS IN B.C. COASTAL WATERS
speechtext:
I realize that the service is still not on a day to day basis; nevertheless my hon. friend has the privilege of representing a riding which has a road in it and now, for the first time, passenger cars and private individuals are enabled to travel out to the Pacific ocean. This is the only road in Canada that takes you to the Pacific ocean. The rest of us only reach the inside passage. One of the things that the withdrawal of these old vessels has accomplished, as new methods of transportation, has been the construction of a growing shift in the roadways which now reach out to the Pacific coast.
I suggest that if we had protected these old vessels by legislation, this new system of transport which now enables people to move freely in and out of Port Alberni would not be available now. I want to cite a further instance. The government of British Columbia, for which I hold no brief has done a rather excellent job in improving ferry services. This new ferry service to Vancouver Island, connecting with the riding of my hon. friend, has replaced the ancient and creeking machinery of the Canadian Pacific which formerly took

a long time to render service to him and to the people of his riding. I suggest it was the competitive spirit of the people living on the coast and in British Columbia which felt that that was necessary to improve upon the facilities serving my hon. friend's riding.
Had the hon. member been able to get his bill through a few years ago, the cloak of protection would have been cast around the shaking shoulders of the old Canadian Pacific. These ancient vessels would still be plying back and forth across the Georgia strait. We would all be cursing and gnashing our teeth, wishing for something better, and talking about building tunnels and bridges. Instead of that, local competition has built new and good services. I suggest that we let her rip, my friend; let these people fight it out and provide better services. Put your faith in free enterprise. Turn your back upon socialism and march forward to victory.

I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, but we are not ready to accept this measure immediately, in view of the fact that, this afternoon, within five minutes, the house passed Bill No. C-99, thereby voting an amount of $8,837,000 and some odd dollars, and that, according to the Bank Act, that amount only represents a cash 20220-220
Bank Act
reserve of $883,700 on the part of the chartered banks. It may then be realized that, before extending the application of the Bank Act and the Quebec Savings Banks Act, the Bank Act must be explained to certain hon. members.
We have raised that question many times, and several hon. members said the Social Crediters were talking through their hats. However, I am under the impression that several hon. members have never read the Bank Act and that they have no idea of what its consequences might be.
That is why I feel that those who may not be familiar with the Bank Act should be told what it is all about, and it is for their information that I will say a few words about it. I can assure the house that in doing so I have no intention of delaying either the passage of this bill or any other business of the house. But since we are especially interested in chartered banks, I thought I should say a few words at this time.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to call the attention of the house on the following quotation of Pius XI's encyclical Quadragesimo Anno:
In the first place, then, It is patent that in our days not alone is wealth accumulated, but immense power and despotic economic domination is concentrated in the hands of a few, and that those few are frequently not the owners, but only the trustees and directors of invested funds, who administer them at their good pleasure.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps it would be appropriate to call hon. members' attention on chapter 48 of the 1953-54 Statutes of Canada, 2-3 Elizabeth II, and to read the definitions given under the heading "Interpretation". I am sure they would be quite surprised by what they would find out.
I should like to point out that this has to do with the legislation on banks and banking operations, but I must say that the Bank Act and the Quebec Savings Banks Act are two different things entirely. As a matter of fact, the Bank Act is recorded in chapter 48 while the Quebec Savings Banks Act is in chapter 41 of the same statutes.
And here is what can be found in section 2 of chapter 48:	"agricultural equipment",
"agricultural implements". And then the definition of a bank follows. Subparagraph C of section 2 says:
"Bank" means the bank to which this act applies.
And then it goes on with the definition of various terms used in the Bank Act, such as "bill of lading", "branch", "corporation controlled by the bank", "farm", "farm electric system", "farmer", "fish", "fisherman", "fishing", "fishing equipment and supplies", "fishing vessel", "goods, wares and merchandise",

Bank Act
"grain", "hydrocarbons", "inspector", "live stock", "manufacturer", etc.
That means that the Bank Act is quite clear and that we are justified in wondering from the beginning what is the purpose of all those definitions.
Mr. Speaker, when we, members of the Social Credit party, say that chartered banks can create credit, that is do something with nothing, when we say that chartered banks can create credit which is 10 or 12 times the amount of their cash reserve, we are told that we talk through our hats.
And yet, if one refers to section 71 of the Bank Act, one can read the following:
The bank shall maintain a cash reserve in the form of a deposit with the Bank of Canada and of Bank of Canada notes held by the bank, and such reserve shall be not less on the average-
-and please note that it does not say more,
-shall be not less on the average during any month than 8 per cent, or such other percentage as may be fixed by the Bank of Canada under the provisions of the Bank of Canada Act.
The chartered banks legislation refers to the Bank of Canada Act, so that we have to consult another act to know exactly the problem of the cash reserve of chartered banks.
And if one looks up the Bank of Canada Act, which is chapter 13 of the 1934 statutes, one can see that section 24 deals with the reserve chartered banks must maintain.
Mr. Speaker, I shall not read everything which concerns this matter, for there are two pages.
In 1954, the act was amended under chapter 33, and section 11 says:
Section 24 of the said act is repealed.
This means that everything in section 24 was repealed, everything concerning the provision of fixed cash or numerary reserves was eliminated because section 24 had been repealed.
Section 28 is repealed and replaced by the next section which becomes section 24. That section mentions a reserve to be maintained by the banks-and this, Mr. Speaker, is in the Bank of Canada Act, not in the Bank Act concerning the chartered banks.
It is very easy to compute the amount of numerary reserves to be held by the banks; I can immediately prove it by quoting subsection 2 of section 71:
For the purpose of determining the amount of the cash reserve required to be maintained by a bank during any month,
(a)	the amount of its deposit liabilities payable in Canadian currency shall be the average of such deposit liabilities at the close of business on Wednesdays in each of the four consecutive weeks ending with the last Wednesday but one in the preceding month,
(b)	the amount of Bank of Canada notes held by the bank shall be the average holdings of such

notes at the close of business on Wednesdays in each of the four consecutive weeks ending with the last Wednesday but one in the preceding month, and
(e) the amount of its deposit with the Bank of Canada shall be the average amount of such deposit at the close of business on each juridical day of the current month.
I know that many members of the house are experts, but it is really difficult to know what are the average cash reserves the chartered banks are supposed to keep. However, they are well protected by the law, I may assure you.
(3) If the property and assets of the Bank of Canada are insufficient to pay its debts and liabilities and the Bank of Canada suspends payments of any of its liabilities, the deposit made under this section by every bank is hereby guaranteed, and the governor in council, on the recommendation of the minister, shall authorize payment out of the consolidated revenue fund of such moneys as are necessary to implement the guarantee.
That is why we have been saying that the banks have discretionary powers, incomparable powers. We would like to see this act amended in some way, so that the people are dealt with a little more justly.
Now, you know what a bank is: the act tells us "Bank means a bank to which this act applies".
What are the powers and business of the banks?
I read this in section 75, and you will see it is very important:
The bank may
(a)	open branches;
It is a great privilege and it is very convenient for banks to open branches.
(b)	acquire, deal in, discount, and lend money and make advances upon the security of, and take as security for any loan or advance made by it, bills of exchange, etc-
I shall not go any further, Mr. Speaker, but I meant to show that the banks are entitled to make loans from 10 to 12 times the amount they have as a reserve in cash on deposit in the Bank of Canada.
The law says so; it is neither us nor even Messrs. Towers, Rasminsky or Coyne. It goes to show that banks have extraordinary powers.
Do you think it would be to one's advantage to be a director of a chartered bank? It could be, because according to the Directory of Directors published by the Financial Post of Canada for 1962, people of very good families, of very good reputation, are chartered bank directors and, at the same time, probably by accident, control more or less directly many companies. I will not quote the whole Directory of Directors, it would be too long and, besides, my time would not suffice. However, I will read the names of some very

decent persons who have succeeded well in business, and I would have done the same thing if the opportunity had arisen.
For instance, in the Bank of Montreal there are: Hon. C. Wallace, director of the Bank of Montreal, who partially controls 16 companies; Hon. H. de M. Molson, also director of the Bank of Montreal, who partially controls nine companies; Hon. Sir Leonard Outer-bridge, who partially controls two companies; Hon. James Sinclair, who partially controls seven companies; Hon. Leslie M. Frost, who partially controls eight companies.
For the Bank of Nova Scotia: Hon. E. Asse-lin, who partially controls 11 companies; Hon. S. A. Hayden, who partially controls six companies.
For the Canadian National Bank: Hon. J. M. Dessureault who partially controls five companies; Hon. F. Philippe Brais, who partially controls 14 companies; Hon. Jean Raymond, who partially controls 32 companies.
For the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce: Hon. G. P. Campbell, who partially controls 37 companies; R. H. Winters, who partially controls 20 companies; Hon. G. B. Foster, who partially controls 35 companies; Hon. J. V. Clyne, who partially controls five companies; Hon. F. M. Ross, who partially controls four companies; Hon. C. C. Pratt, who partially controls 15 companies.
For the Royal Bank: Hon. Paul H. Bouffard, who partially controls 19 companies.
For the Toronto-Dominion Bank: Hon. J. A. Mathewson, who partially controls ten companies.
For the Provincial Bank of Canada: Hon. J. Olier Renaud, who partially controls five companies; Hon. Gerald Martineau, who partially controls seven companies; and formerly, Hon. Lionel Chevrier, who partially controlled three companies.
That was taken from the Directory of Directors for 1962. I checked the 1963 edition: the name of Mr. Lionel Chevrier has been deleted; the name of the Hon. Louis S. St. Laurent, who controls Famous Players Corporation is there, but no mention is made of the fact that he is a director of that company.
However, the 1963 edition mentions Mr. Roger Letourneau, big fund raiser of the Quebec Liberal party, director of the Bank of Montreal and associated with nine companies; Mr. Peter Nesbitt Thompson who was secretary treasurer of the Quebec Liberal federation and who is director of 49 companies, excluding the Canadian Oil Co. that he sold to American interests. Moreover, we saw yesterday or the day before that he had just been appointed director of the Greater Winnipeg Gas Company. Finally, there is Mr. Renault 20220-220i
Bank Act
St. Laurent, son of the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, who is director of the Canadian National Bank and who plays a part in the control of the destiny of ten other companies.
Mr. Speaker, as you can see, it is rather important to know where the privilege granted by the Bank Act, the chartered banks act and the Bank of Canada Act can lead.
As Pope Pius XI stated:
That is how in a manner of speaking they pump blood into the economic organism whose life they hold in their hands in such a way that without their consent no one can no longer breathe and only the strongest survive.
That is to say that the ones who are most determined in the fight are those who are less hampered by their conscience.
The issue is quite serious and the people cast the chain of their own enslavement because they are unaware of the power of high finance.
It is all very well to speak of planning, state control, crown corporations and what not, but no effort is made to find out the true causes of the problem.
Lately, a federal member pointed out to me that the Russian revolution, which took place in 1917, was quite satisfied with the banking system for many years since banks were only nationalized in 1935. It goes to show that even under a socialist or communist system banks are still sufficiently strong to keep on controlling the economy.
Some statements in the Porter commission's report are, to say the least, unfounded. In the first place, on pages 112 and 113, it is stated that banks create credit. We see it repeatedly written in legislation. People say it is not true. But, we see it in the Porter commission's report; not bad, for a start.
It is further stated that, with the exception of existing chartered banks, banking institutions should be allowed to make unsecured loans to individuals and enterprises in addition to loans secured under section 88.
Those amendments would increase competition and, at the same time, give the institutions more freedom to specialize as they see fit, thus improving at lesser cost their services to the community as a whole.
Without entering into an argument, I should like to say that such a reason is absolutely false and inadmissible.
This is what was said about cash reserves:
Perhaps it would be appropriate to reduce them a little further.
About foreign banks in Canada, it says:
It would be possible to have regulations to prevent foreign banks to assume control in Canada.
That is to say, we could see to it that they do not take over Canadian banks.
And the commission recommends:
That any purchase of shares in Canadian banks by foreign banks be subject to approval by the treasury board.

Bank Act
It considers abnormal that the government exercises no control whatever on purchases made by foreign banks, whereas it forbids or at least regulates such action by Canadian institutions.
Therefore, as you can see, Mr. Speaker, the question of extending by one year the application of the Bank Act is extremely important.
I understand the banks would suspend their banking operations on July 1 if the bill is not passed. I can tell the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) right now that it will be accepted, because it is a fait accompli. We keep, accepting accomplished facts in this House of Commons. We pass postdated bills, so to speak, for expenditures made six months ago.
We agree with the new legislation, but we want the hon. members who did not have time to examine the Bank Act to know right away that, when the time comes to really amend that act, we shall come forward with very strong arguments and, above all, we will not let the legislation pass if some of our recommendations are not accepted.
The Porter commission report also says this:
The commission thus maintains it would be beneficial to the economy if the interest rates asked by the Farm Credit Corporation and the industrial development bank were to follow more closely the rates on the financial markets, so as not to cripple the operations of private lenders.
Mr. Speaker, those agencies were established by parliament to assist the farmers, large and small, in short, to help farmers and industrialists with an average capital benefit from capital funds at a reasonable interest rate.
The Porter commission-and I shall not give the names of its members, because anybody can find them in the new book just published on the subject, but some of them are bankers-the Porter commission, as I say, is asking that interest rates be raised. Of course, the role played by those organizations then becomes worthless, if the recommendation of the Porter commission is carried out.
The Porter commission also points out:
*-that the financial situation of the provinces and of most of the municipalities is generally sound in spite of their substantial deficits in the last few years.
Is that logical? They have experienced in the last few years substantial deficits, but their financial situation is sound.
Some small municipalities have greater difficulties in getting funds than their financial situation could warrant.
That is for sure. Montreal, Toronto and few other large cities excepted, there is hardly one single municipality in a borrowing position.

It says here some small municipalities but I think that we could easily change "some" to "thousands".
But the provincial governments could often remedy that situation in helping them to supply a more complete and more up to date information for the securities purchasers.
Here, it is practically suggested that municipalities resort to some advertising; but municipalities such as that of Saint-Marc-des-Car-rieres, Beauport or others are unable to do so because they cannot get any credit.
So, as I said, I find that the report of the Porter commission contains some recommendations which are unacceptable.
I shall not go any further in this field. But I would simply like to quote an excerpt from the speech made by the hon. member for St. Maurice-Lafleche (Mr. Chretien), on May 12 last, as reported in Hansard, page 3186, when the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau) asked him why the recommendations set forth by the royal commission on banking appointed in 1944 had not yet been put into practice. The hon. member for St. Maurice-Lafleche then answered as follows:
I am pleased to answer this question of the hon. member for Shefford. A commission can make recommendations that the government may find unacceptable. And when we have responsible government like the one we then had, it is possible that it decided not to accept them in the political climate that prevailed at the time.
I hope and trust that many recommendations of the Porter commission will not be accepted as they stand now, because that would be detrimental to the Canadian people.
Now, as for the power of banks to create credit, that power is given to them, not alone, but with the power to charge interest also. The fact is that the Canadian government itself is faced with an extraordinary problem, because it has a considerable debt and it must pay fantastic amounts in interests alone.
In the first volume of Public Accounts of Canada for the year 1963, it is said that the amount paid in 1962-63 was $881,598,898 in interest alone.
Now we know that the deficit for that same year amounted to $691,632,927, which means that we paid $200 million more than the debt interest deficit. That is, if we did not have any interest to pay to the banks, we could get rid of our deficit and register a surplus of $200 million for 1962-1963.
Now, some hon. members are saying: If our financing was without interest, it would get us nowhere.
Well, Mr. Speaker, if this is the only thing that worries them, we are ready even to accept that the government pay some interest -I, at least, am ready to do so; but let the government pay it not to individuals, not to

those who are living from interest paid on money loaned, but to the Canadian people. There would not be any problem then, and we could pay 6 per cent, except that the money would return to the consolidated fund of the Canadian government.
Therefore, if that is enough to make it clear to people that they should use the money of the Bank of Canada, we are willing to make this concession and to accept that the interest be paid to the Canadian people.
I shall now revert to the matter of interest. The interest of the federal government is one thing, but there is also the interest paid by municipalities. In my own city of Beauport, as reported in the newspaper L'Action of March 21, 1963, the debt charges cost $184,600, which means that the percentage of the debt compared to the estimates is 41.76 per cent.
It is strange that 41.76 per cent of taxes paid by individual taxpayers are used to service the debt.
As recently as May 8, 1964, I read in Le Droit of Ottawa that the budget of the municipality of Eastview included $262,200 for debt service. Those are fantastic amounts given to people creating credit. This credit is not provided by means of some people's savings so as to benefit others, but it is created out of nothing and made available to other people. In doing so, they make a profit.
Now, the report of the Porter commission maintains that:
About 30 per cent of the credits of $100,000 or more granted by the banks at the end of 1962 were for the benefit of their directors, or of firms or companies in which they were also shareholders or directors, or of borrowers of whom they were surety.
Mr. Speaker, we can see that our system is well organized and, from memory, I could quote an export insurance company-you know that the government votes amounts for an insurance company to guarantee the payment of exports-which is now and has been for some years under the control of the chartered banks. This means that the chartered banks create credit and make loans which the people will have to repay. This is why they are sure that this amount will be paid, for if foreign countries refuse to pay, the government guarantees to them the payment of the amount involved.
I do not wish to dwell any more on the subject, for there are so many things which could be said. I simply wanted to show the members of the house who cannot conduct research that there are perhaps in the position we take justifiable points. If others wish more detail, they may ask questions. As far as we are concerned, no doubt we shall revert to the matter when the chartered banks act is introduced next year.

maintopic: BANK ACT-QUEBEC SAVINGS BANKS ACT EXTENSION FOR ONE YEAR OF AUTHORITY TO CARRY ON BUSINESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have to congratulate my colleague, the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Marcoux), whose very explicit statement may, I believe, have opened the eyes of many hon. members.
Under the circumstances, I feel that it is reasonable to pass this legislation now under consideration, the purpose of which is to amend the Bank Act and to extend for a year, that is up to July 1, 1965, the privilege of the banks to issue currency, that is to create ex nihilo the credit which is the only currency now in circulation in Canada, because even bank notes and metallic currency are bought at the Bank of Canada with a mere draft drawn on their account at the Bank of Canada and accumulated through credits previously created.
We are in favour of this bill, because it is absolutely necessary for all hon. members to have enough time available for a thorough study of our Canadian banking system. Yet, they all must co-operate and, first of all, get rid of their prejudices, and lift the veil of mystery which covers the Canadian monetary system. How many hon. members have actually conducted any research in depth with regard to the historical background and the evolution and operation of our financial system? Their number is certainly very restricted.
A year would hardly be too much to enable all hon. members to contribute as individuals to the improvement of our banking system. I would, indeed think it extremely desirable for all Canadians together, putting aside all political considerations, to come, a year from now to the conclusion that it would be fitting for the Canadian government to recover the royal privilege which never should have been ceded, when the Bank Act was amended in 1870 and in 1871, and which maintained for the chartered banks the special privilege of printing bank notes and issuing credit.
In reality, the issuance of credit is a sovereign power lent to the commercial banks, but the time has come for the federal state to recover that right to issue credit through the Bank of Canada.
With confederation, the provinces gave to the central government the exclusive right to legislate in monetary matters. Why did the federal state, even after the setting up of the Bank of Canada, leave to a private sector of our economy, that is to the chartered banks, the prerogatives of bank credits. That is something absolutely inconceivable that the most important operation, the issuance of credit or the creation of new money, be left in the hands of chartered banks. '
Only parliament has the power to amend the chartered banks' act and that is why

Bank Act
even if in a year's time, we passed only one item of legislation giving back to the Bank of Canada the absolute power to issue credit, to coin the resources of Canada for the benefit of all Canadians, it would be infinitely better than a great number of meaningless pieces of legislation passed these last 25 years, because they only evaded the problem of a stagnant economy and a galloping inflation.
Our monetary system is essentially inflationary in character. Canada cannot go on stagnating in a financial system that gives us deficit budgets, an exhausted treasury, monetary instability, continuous depreciation of our currency, lack of currency, exchange control, high cost of money, multiplicity of taxes, nuisance taxes, and finally credit anarchy. Whether it concerns a nation or a business, any sound administration must obey a rigid set of rules. For that purpose, we must regulate the financial activity of the country and also the national economic activity.
Someone just handed me a document showing that inflation does exist in most countries of the world at the present time. Even the common market has to declare war on inflation. Canada is not the only country faced with inflation; there is inflation in all countries which have adopted the same financial system. There is inflation in Brazil and also in other countries. The Minister of Finance is now waiting for something and I am under the impression that he is looking for new solutions to free the country from the financial trap which stifles Canadians. In his last budget, he stopped the increase of taxes, but for how long?
I take this opportunity to tell the Minister of Finance that I support his policy aimed at freeing our country from foreign capital, and I prefer the nationalism of a Walter Gordon to the internationalism of Eric Kierans who, with the policy he advocates, is one of the worst masters of the inflation and depreciation of our currency.
Nationalism is not an exaggerated desire for power, but on the contrary it is the will to maintain and develop what is necessary to the life of the community.
Mr. Speaker, from the end of 1954 to July 1, 1963, monetary inflation increased in a dangerous way. Indeed, during that period, borrowings on foreign financial markets by municipal, provincial and federal governments as well as by private companies totalled $5,140 million. During that time, foreign investments in Canada reached $13,950 million.
Furthermore, if we add to those amounts, the amount of the new credits issued by

chartered banks during the same period, amounting to $5,248 million, we have a grand total of $24,338 million of debt money put into circulation in Canada over a period of eight years and six months. That is aberration at its worst. On the other hand, when an economic system needs artificial means to function, it is basically unsound, and this bill will give us ample time to rectify the matter. Statistics on consumer credit show that, at December 31,	1963, there were
$6,604,000,000 in loans to finance consumer goods. That figure does not cover instalment purchases, accounts and credit cards of all kinds.
It is by hundreds of millions of dollars that chartered banks create credit for the loan companies which finance consumption. In addition, they must also finance consumption themselves, because consumers do not have enough money to buy goods. That is a new factor which contributes to disastrous inflation in our country. It is precisely in such circumstances that violent economic crises occur; if that is so, it is because instead of merely financing production, an artificial purchasing power is based on the hope of meeting monthly instalments rather than on the true purchasing power at the time of purchase or on previous savings. Indeed, that is a frightening situation if you consider the interest rate on all those consumer loans.
That proves once again the necessity of amending the Bank Act, because when a country such as Canada cannot give a lasting value to its currency, cannot balance its budget and only succeeds in increasing its debts, it is easy to see that we are going around in a vicious circle.
Financial balance and the stability of monetary value can never be achieved as long as parliament does not give the Bank of Canada, this bank of banks, the regalities which it should have logically and naturally, and as long as a distinction is not made between social investment expenditures or public investment expenditures, which provide the funds required for the national equipment, and the commercial capital meant to boost the agricultural, industrial and commercial activities.
Thus, thanks to the bill which is now before us, we 'will be able to prepare within a year the necessary monetary reform. It will then be possible to achieve such a reform quite easily by amending the Bank Act in such a way as to provide that henceforth the Bank of Canada would have the privilege of creating credit. It would not be more difficult than that. Thus, any credit would be based on values under the control of a national credit

council with representatives from the Bank of Canada, the major financial institutions, including the credit unions and the major intermediate agencies.
As for the methods of application of banking practice concerning the rediscount of banking instruments which could be granted to all banks and credit unions-and I insist on that-that is a matter of internal administration that the national credit board could change. However, I wish to point out that the maximum interest rate on loans made by banks as well as credit unions, should never, under any circumstances, exceed 5 per cent.
I add that the Bank of Canada would be authorized to grant credit without interest or at cost to the government of Canada for the financing of public capital works or social services, always under the control of the national credit board, so that those treasury operations could be made according to criteria corresponding to statistics. That procedure would be a scientifically controlled release of purchasing power directly to the public and would constitute a reversal of the monetary circulation to finance consumption. In our present system, credit is generally issued in order to finance a new production, while there is no money in circulation to buy the former production.
From now on the Bank of Canada would look after the financing of treasury bills, if any, at administrative cost.
Finally, the municipal credit bank, connected with the Bank of Canada, would replace the municipal loan fund and would grant loans to municipalities at administrative cost, accepting their bonds as security. It would be a very simple machinery which would upset nothing and which would put everything back in order, allowing the economy to operate smoothly.
What would result from the implementation of those financial proposals? We would witness a gradual decrease in municipal taxes, a reduction of federal and provincial taxes, a revalorization of our currency and, finally, a drop in the cost of living. The various governments would be able to balance their budget. There would be work and income for everyone, and coercion and centralization under any form would disappear.
If, on the contrary, the federal government maintains its policy of impoverishment of the Canadian people and of depreciation of all our values, there will no longer be any hope of establishing a truly binational confederation, and the federal administration will remain under a financial tyranny when it could become free so easily.

subtopic: LEGISLATION RESPECTING TERRITORIAL WATERS AND FISHERIES LAWS

speechtext: The house resumed from Wednesday, May 20, consideration of the motion of Mr. Martin (Essex East) for the second reading of Bill No. S-17, respecting the territorial sea and fishing zones of Canada.

subtopic: LEGISLATION RESPECTING TERRITORIAL WATERS AND FISHERIES LAWS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
at five o'clock yesterday, when this item was last up for consideration, I was nearing the end of my remarks, but I referred to statements which had been made during the last election campaign with regard to this very important matter of the protection of our coastal waters for the exclusive use of our fishermen, so far as that may be possible.
I note that these comments have gone back over the years, indeed over the last three election campaigns. Speaking in Yarmouth on March 14, 1958, the present Prime Minister was reported as follows:
Mr. Pearson's most important proposal.. .was a strong endorsement of the extension of Canadian territorial waters from the present three mile limit to 12 miles. This would oiler Canadian fishermen much greater protection from foreign fishing vessels.
He said that in spite of the fact both Britain and the United States are opposed to it Canada should continue to press for this extension due to the international conference next fall.

Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones I do not know to which conference he could have been referring, because when that statement was made the very important law of the sea conference of 1958 was then going on in Geneva. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that the two conferences on the law of the sea took place in the intervening period between that and the 1962 campaign, one in 1958 and one in 1960, and in the interval the government of the day was trying by every means possible to reach agreement so that we might extend our exclusive fishing zones.
As I have already said, this business of legislating with regard to nationals of other countries on what we admit is part of the high seas, is a very questionable procedure.
I reiterate that I hope it will succeed, but it is a difficult thing unless we have the cooperation and agreement of some of the most important countries involved which have a stake in this matter.
I shall try to keep my remarks as brief as possible, but I would like to point out that this became a political issue, or attempts were made to make it a political issue. With reference to the 1962 election campaign, reporting a speech that the Prime Minister made in Charlottetown, the Toronto Telegram said:
He also made his first formal promise of the campaign. A Liberal government, he pledged, would institute a 12 mile limit (to replace the existing three mile limit) unilaterally, if a 12 mile limit could not be achieved through nter-national agreement.
This was repeated many times, and an attempt was made to create the illusion in the minds of those listening to these speeches that if the present Prime Minister were granted the magic power of being Prime Minister, all he had to do was wave some magic wand and all these foreign vessels would disappear over the horizon and never be seen again. It was as simple as that.
For example, speaking in Sydney during the last election campaign in 1963 he said:
-we as a Canadian government will declare a 12 mile limit by national action.. .I'm not afraid of this step-the present government is.
Mr. Speaker, the former government, referred to in that context as the "present government", was not afraid to take action. I must say I have great respect for bravery, but I have learned over the years to have great misgivings about foolhardiness and it would be a terrible mistake if, by doing something brash, we antagonize our friends to the point where they would make it as difficult as possible for us to attain our objectives.
These speeches by the Prime Minister went on indefinitely, and I think they were unfortunate because an attempt was made to create the impression in the minds of our

fishermen that a 12 mile zone could be set aside exclusively for their own use. This is virtually an impossibility because there are a number of treaty rights and other things which have to be taken into consideration.
In this connection, when the Prime Minister's formal pledge was first made in 1962,
I read this quotation from a report of the occasion:
During supper in Charlottetown, the Liberal leader read over his speech for that night and added a final paragraph. It was a tricky ending for a political address-a few sentences on political morality reinforced with quotes from Wesley and a modern Catholic philosopher and theologian- but it worked beautifully.
I must say it did not work because the people I represent are shrewd, and they were not taken in by this. I am not sure to which Wesley he was referring. It may have been a former member, Mr. Wesley Stewart. On the other hand, if he was talking about John Wesley, I am sure John Wesley must have turned over in his grave when that statement was made.

speechtext:
That would figure. Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to conclude because I know there are other members who wish to participate in this debate. I am not even attempting to mention a number of important factors, such as the problem of enforcement that may be involved, but I am sure this will be covered by other hon. members.
I am pleased that the Secretary of State for External Affairs indicated that the bill would be referred to the standing committee on marine and fisheries. I think this is an important piece of legislation which should be examined thoroughly by the committee and I welcome the expression of intention in this regard. However, I want to say this: A promise was made by the party now in power that within a year a 12 mile exclusive fishing zone would be instituted. An attempt was made to imply that this 12 mile zone would be for the exclusive use of Canadian fishermen. What is the state of affairs? Legislation is being brought in at this time, but because negotiations are still continuing we do not know what concessions we shall have to make to other countries in order to get their acquiescence in this. Both the minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) are reported to have said in Washington on December 5, 1963-I have a report here which perhaps I could read:
Both External Affairs Minister Paul Martin and Fisheries Minister Hedard A. Robichaud said here yesterday that historic rights of United States

fishermen will not be affected when Canada establishes a 12 mile national fishing zone as it is proposed to do next mid-May.
I do not always depend completely on the accuracy of such reports, but there is no doubt about it that France and the United States have treaty rights which will have to be respected. So we shall have these exceptions. Then there are the traditional fishing rights of a number of countries. We do not know where we stand with regard to these, or at least I do not, because the negotiations are still going on. But I should be surprised if we were not obliged to make considerable concessions along the lines of a phasing out period. This, too, will be in the nature of an exception to the suggested exclusion.
Moreover, until the orders in council establishing the geographical co-ordinates are passed we shall not know where the base line is to be or what bodies of water will lie behind them and thus become national waters. I think this is bad practice. It is unfortunate that the effect of the bill which, after all, is the important thing, will occur at some time in the future when the government will not be obligated to bring the matter before parliament. It will be a fait accompli. Not until the negotiations are complete and the government is ready to pass the order in council will we know the effect of what we are doing now. We are buying, as it were, a pig in a poke. We do not know what concessions we may have to make in order to get any agreement at all.
My final point is this: The law itself, of course, will not become effective until its proclamation and no fixed date for proclamation is given in the bill. We have no means of knowing when this act is to be proclaimed and we therefore have no means of knowing when it will become effective. I hope that when the minister speaks he will be able to enlighten us on some of these points. When the act is proclaimed, the only effect it will have is to become a statement of Canada's determination to establish an exclusive fishing zone, with certain exceptions, out beyond our present territorial waters. Then, when the co-ordinates are established at a later date these will presumably have a bearing on what will become our national waters.
So I regret we are passing this legislation now. However, if it will strengthen the hand of the government in its negotiations with other countries we are willing to support it on that basis at this time. But a far more logical process, to my mind, would have been for the government to have completed its negotiations and then, based on what they had been able to do, to have brought a bill before us and told us frankly what had been the result of the negotiations and what concessions we
Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones had been obliged to make. Then we would know where we stood in the matter. This, in, my judgment, would be far more acceptable from a parliamentary point of view. Under the present arrangement parliament is being asked, as it were, to sign a blank cheque and trust to luck.
I think, frankly, that the reason this is being done at the present time is to create the illusion that we have reached some special milepost-and we have not. I do not think so, anyway. These negotiations, as the government has found, are long and difficult; people who do not wish to agree can stall and keep coming back to negotiate again and again. It is slow progress. When the former government were trying to safeguard Canada's interests by negotiating patiently but actively in this field we were accused of not doing anything- of having no will to succeed in this endeavour. This was not the fact, and I deplore the situation which has brought about the somewhat premature presentation of this legislation to parliament. Nevertheless, on behalf of the official opposition I wish the government every success in these negotiations. We hope they will be fruitful. We have witnessed this spectacle of promises made in the heat of election campaigns. They sounded good-as if this was as simple a matter as could be imagined; as if when the present Prime Minister came to office all he had to do was say the word and these foreign fishing vessels would disappear over the horizon forever. Now we see the Secretary of State for External Affairs in the role of sorcerer's apprentice trying to make it appear as though we were achieving this result. That is the aspect of the legislation which I deplore.
I have only one further comment to make. No matter how successful we may be in these negotiations, even if we succeed in our objectives, there is a still more important factor yet as far as the fisheries, particularly in the Pacific, are concerned. I refer to the general problem of the conservation of the resources of the high seas. In this connection I should like to quote briefly from a statement made by a member of the Canadian delegation at the Geneva conference in 1958. The representative was Mr. Ozere, the present assistant deputy minister of fisheries, and I quote his remarks because what he says is self-evident when one is familiar with the facts of this matter. Here is the extract from the record:
Mr. Ozere (Canada) observed that, whatever understanding might be reached on the extent of the territorial sea or the contiguous zones, there would remain many problems affecting the conservation and management of sea fisheries which would not be solved by the simple formula of drawing lines in the seas. That was not to say that the adoption of an exclusive fishing zone would not be of definite benefit to those countries which, like his own-

Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones That is, Canada:
-had developed their fisheries mainly along their own coasts.
That is the situation, exactly, as I see it; I think that states it well. I wish the government success in these negotiations and in the other inevitable negotiations with regard to the conservation and exploitation of the living resources of the sea.

Mr. Speaker, I should like at the outset to say that I agree with the views which have just been expressed by the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) about the weaknesses of this bill as far as the absence of any determination of the base lines that are to be fixed is concerned. He referred to the bill as being a pig in a poke, and I intend to say something further on that aspect of the matter later on in my remarks. I hope to find that the hon. member is prepared to support my contentions in this connection.
Actually, when this bill was introduced by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) with his usual verbosity and enthusiasm, I must say the thought that crossed my mind was that the bill was a bit like the proverbial bride's first cake. While it may be a little difficult to imagine the Secretary of State for External Affairs as the blushing bride rushing in with the cake to show it off to hubby, nevertheless that was the thought that crossed my mind as he was introducing this bill. The unfortunate thing, it seems to me, is that the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the government, in their hurry to produce this first cake have become a bit flustered and have left out of the bill, or the cake, a good many of the essential ingredients. In fact it seems to me there is really nothing in the make-up of the bill but flour and water, and therefore the result is really not much of a cake.
I certainly agree with the remarks of the Secretary of State for External Affairs and with those made by the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) as to the importance of the subject matter that is dealt with in this bill. A bill which has to do with the matter of the territorial sea and fishing zone of Canada is, in my view, a matter of importance not only to the people who live in the coastal areas of Canada but to the entire nation. Much has been said about the importance of the living resources of the sea in a world where the population is growing apace and where an increasing shortage of high protein foods becomes ever more evident. I think it is in the context of that kind of situation that at least the subject matter of this bill should be considered, even though in my view the importance of the bill which has been presented falls


a long way short of measuring up to the importance of the subject matter.
The hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) referred to the bravery of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) with regard to some statements he had made in the Atlantic areas of the country in reference to the declaration of a 12 mile fishing zone for Canada. As far as I am concerned, thinking back to the days when I was first in the house, when some of us from over here were advocating the desirability of a firm course of action by Canada in this connection, the brave words of the Prime Minister certainly represented a good step forward. But, of course, I am sure the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) will agree with me that from our experience and observation we always find that the Liberal party and its leader are much braver when they are in opposition than when they are on the side of the house to the right of Mr. Speaker.
Consequently, now that we have this bill before us we find there has taken place a considerable retreat from some of the bolder words that were uttered by the Prime Minister on the occasion to which the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) referred.
We in the New Democratic party have been attempting to follow all the recent developments in this situation as closely as we can. Reference has already been made to the United Nations conferences on the law of the sea in 1958 and 1960 and of the failure there to reach international agreement on this subject matter by the required two thirds majority in a vote. I am not going to expand upon that situation, except to say that it has, of course, made quite evident the fact that if anything is to happen in this context, some action along the lines of the declaration of the Prime Minister for the establishment of a fishing zone for Canada needs to be taken.
We have advocated that this action should perhaps have been taken earlier than it was, while recognizing of course that there is a great deal of need for international co-operation in this area. However, as far as we are concerned we believe that the real area in which international negotiation, international treaty and international understanding is required lies in the high seas problems as far as the fishery is concerned to a much greater extent than it does in connection with the establishment of a coastal fishing zone. We believe, also, that in the light of the action which has already been taken by a very larger number of the nations of the world, Canada certainly is well within her rights in taking a firm position in this connection.
During the period since this announcement was made by the Prime Minister, and since we have been informed in our questions to the Secretary of State for External Affairs

and to the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Robi-chaud) that negotiations have been going on, we have been very much concerned as to the progress of these negotiations. We have been quite concerned that these negotiations appear to have become quite protracted. I am not prepared at the moment to pass any severe judgment upon the Canadian negotiators in this field because the negotiations have not been sooner brought to a determination, desirable though I feel that would have been; but during the period when we were addressing questions to the government on this subject we rather assumed from the answers that were being given to us-perhaps we took this too easily for granted-that the government would not be bringing any legislation before parliament on this subject until these negotiations were concluded. Obviously we wrongly assumed that this would be the case. Naturally we took it for granted that the government would expect parliament to have the substance of the matter before it before we were asked to approve legislation, so that at least we would be intelligently informed and would know what we were talking about.
Rather to my surprise I found that the legislation was being introduced in the other place and would only reach this house following consideration there. This certainly came as a surprise to me and in many ways served rather to mislead those of us who were particularly concerned in this matter, because we had assumed that this legislation would be introduced in this house, where it could be initially dealt with either by the Secretary of State for External Affairs or the Minister of Fisheries.
Some of the inadequacies of the bill have already been pointed out by the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean). I will not attempt to repeat them in detail, but I think there is substance in the point he made to the effect that the real significance of this change in our territorial sea and fishing zones lies much more in where the straight base lines are established than it does in the nine mile fishing fringe which will lie outside the area designated as our territorial sea.
As far as I can see, in the absence of any determination of that matter all we are getting is a poor skeleton of a bill, something which really does not amount to much more than the pious declaration which has already been made by the Prime Minister of Canada's intentions. The fact that this bill as drafted leaves it entirely in the hands of the governor in council to take action as, when and if he sees fit, on the matter of establishing the straight base lines strikes at the very crux of the principle of the bill as I see it, because

Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones without it the main purport of the subject matter is meaningless to me.
The question of where these base lines will be established was not outlined by the secretary of state when he introduced this bill. I looked at the evidence given by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of Fisheries before the banking and commerce committee of the other place, and as far as I could see from the evidence they gave there, there is no indication given of the intention of the government in this regard. It is true that appended to the minutes of those proceedings is a copy of the brief submitted by the fisheries council of Canada, in which is included a couple of maps indicating the desires of the fisheries council of Canada in this connection. While many of us may agree with the proposals of the fisheries council of Canada, we have had no indication that I recall whether or not the government intends that these base lines should be established either on the Atlantic coast or on the Pacific coast. When one couples that lack of definiteness with the fact that the bill not only provides that these base lines should be set by the governor in council but that they may be changed from time to time by the governor in council as he sees fit, then it appears to me that this present bill is completely unsatisfactory and inadequate.
The subject matter of the bill, as I said earlier, is in my view of extreme importance. It certainly requires a much greater and more detailed consideration in this committee than it received in the committee of the other place, where many of those who were most interested and concerned in this matter, including the commercial fishermen themselves, were not able to appear and express their point of view.

Well, Mr. Speaker, I do not quarrel with the minister's statement on that matter and I was not expressing any view as to where the responsibility for the situation lies. However, seeing that he has mentioned this question of a week's notice, I do not feel that a week's notice on a matter of this importance is very adequate. If the minister is referring to the organized fishermen on the west coast he probably knows that at that time they happened to be involved in some rather important meetings on the matter of unresolved negotiations with which the minister is quite familiar. But as I say, I was not assessing any blame; I was merely stating the fact that their point of view had not been presented.

Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones
I find it increasingly difficult to understand the rather cavalier attitude which is being taken by the present government with regard to international treaties, particularly those relating to fishing. For example, during the last session I tried to bring to the attention of the house the fact that the international north Pacific fisheries treaty had been amended by the government without any proper notice being given either to this house or to the public of Canada through the medium of the Canada Gazette; that in fact the treaty had been amended as the result of a telephone call from one of the officials of a government department to Vancouver.
The government is now bringing in a bill on this very important subject while it says negotiations are still going on, no indication being given of a reasonable termination date. We are given no indication as to what is the likely outcome of the negotiations either in respect to where the base lines are going to be established or as to whether or not there is going to be any understanding, agreement or decision reached on a termination date to so-called historic rights of nationals of other countries. I gather from the evidence given in the committee of the other place that the government has no intention of attempting to renegotiate any of the treaty rights, although I do not consider that in itself to be as serious as this other question, because apparently the treaty rights are not as significant as they might have been a number of years ago. I do not know whether members from the Atlantic provinces would agree with that. Nevertheless this is the situation in which we are being asked to approve this bill, and I submit, Mr. Speaker, that it is simply not good enough for the government to expect parliament to take definitive action which, as the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) has already said, gives the government a blank cheque to do practically what it likes with regard to where the fishing zones of Canada are going to be. Not only the present government but any future government, if this legislation is passed, will be in the position of being able to manoeuvre and manipulate in this field without coming to parliament for approval.
So, Mr. Speaker, we in this party feel that this bill should not receive approval as it stands. I should like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron):
That Bill S-17 be not now read a second time, but that the subject matter thereof he referred to the standing committee on marine and fisheries for consideration and report.
If this motion carries it means that the marine and fisheries committee of this house, comprised largely of members who are most

interested and concerned in this bill, will be in a position to say, after these negotiations are concluded, when progress reports can be made and to consider and assess what real progress the government is making in this field. If the committee is satisfied with the kind of progress the government has made, it will be able to bring back to the house definitive recommendations as to how a bill should be presented which would clearly set out the areas to be included in the internal waters of Canada and the fishing zones of Canada. We feel that unless this is done before we put anything into final legislative form, we have no guarantee that the rights and interests of the fishermen of this country are going to be adequately protected.

subtopic: LEGISLATION RESPECTING TERRITORIAL WATERS AND FISHERIES LAWS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the debate on this particular measure before us I want to say, first of all, that there are many very serious reservations with regard to it. So far as the general principle is concerned, which of course is what we are mainly considering at the moment, it should receive the support of hon. members. However, I can quite understand the hesitancy with which some members, especially the previous speaker, have approached this particular matter. They have voiced fears that if the measure were passed in its present form it would not, to any extent, meet the needs of our fisheries.
Looking back into the history of this particular matter, we are reminded first of all of a statement that was made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) about one year ago. He stated it was the intention of the government to declare the 12 mile fishing limit in May, 1964. Of course, we are now in May of 1964 and the measure is being presented. At that time comments were made with regard to the statement and it was pointed out in one news article that this was the fulfilment of another Liberal election promise. The article was quite complimentary with regard to this particular matter.
At that time also it was pointed out by others, for instance in the Pacific Troller, the January-February issue, and I quote:
When the Minister of Fisheries, H. J. Robichaud, announced the government's intentions to declare a 12 mile territorial limit in May of 1964, the entire fishing industry was elated with the good news.
The government's announcement was forthright and courageous; it heartened the fishermen's pride in their Minister of Fisheries and renewed our hope for protection from foreign exploitation of our shoreline fisheries which for Canadian fishermen represents practically their entire fishery.
We realize, as has been pointed out by the Secretary of State for External Affairs when he presented this measure, that there are currently about 50 nations that have extended

their limits and Canada is more or less following in the train of those other nations. I believe, therefore, we can welcome the introduction of the bill so far as the general principle is concerned. However, I do join with other members in voicing misgivings over a number of issues that are involved.
First of all, I would reiterate our regret over the continuing hesitancy to place the matter before the committee on marine and fisheries. We have an indication, in this particular instance, that the representations made by the fishermen's unions were not acceptable. As was pointed out tonight, they were not able to make arrangements in time to meet with the committee of the other place. I would suggest that during the past few months there has been ample opportunity for a meeting of the committee on marine and fisheries, even although this measure was not before us, and the fishermen's unions and other organizations would have had ample opportunity to make their views known with regard to the particular issues involved in the introduction of such a measure as this. I feel it is unfortunate that we have the measure before us without having had the opportunity of hearing representations from the fishermen's union and other interested parties.
There has been some discussion concerning the matter of historic fishing rights. As was pointed out by the Secretary of State for External Affairs when he presented this measure on May 20, as recorded on page 3411 of Hansard, there have been discussions with those countries which do possess pre-rights for parts of our shores, namely the United States and France. Then, he said:
We have made clear that the United States and France will be allowed to continue to fish in those areas where they have fished before, subject to agreed arrangements and regulations for the protection of the fisheries concerned.
It has been emphasized, I believe, that there is no intention on the part of the government to alter historic fishing rights. This, it seems to me, creates somewhat of a paradox. In the June 7, 1963 issue of the Montreal Gazette there is one paragraph in an editorial which I should like to read:
There has arisen a new anomaly. For the Canadian government, realizing the need for conservation, has prohibited Canadians from fishing under certain conditions. But foreign ships have been able to move in and fish as they please between the three mile and the 12 mile limit.
Then, the Globe and Mail for December 5, 1963, carried an article from which I should like to quote this paragraph:
This would continue an incongruous arrangement in which Canadian trawlers are prohibited for conservation reasons from fishing in coastal waters which are open to foreign fishermen.
