Notwithstanding the conservation arguments made by Canada at Geneva, the Canadian government's method of relieving this inequity seemingly will be to ease the regulations affecting Canadian trawlers.
This points up the particular situation that seemingly is going to exist where at times Canadian fishermen will be deprived of fishing opportunities while other nations are able to move in and take advantage of them.
Strenuous objections have been raised by the united fishermen and allied workers union which represents a great many of the fishermen of the west coast. They have been very zealous in their representations on behalf of the fishermen and have raised strenuous objections with regard to this particular matter. In their letter of May 14, 1964 they state:
We are absolutely opposed to Bill S-17 and call for its defeat unless it is amended to exclude all foreign fishermen from the 12 mile limit outside a base line which is clearly defined by legislation and not left to be defined or amended by secret orders in council.
In a news release issued by the united fishermen and allied workers union they also emphasize this matter very clearly and strenuously. Sometimes I think the intemperate language used by these organizations in making their representations is more likely to build up walls of resistance than to break them down, but none the less it does indicate how strongly they feel about some of these matters that are not covered in the measure now before us.
A distinction has been drawn between historic rights established by treaty and traditional rights established by traditional fishing practices. In this connection various views have been taken as to what should be done. For instance, the pamphlet, the Pacific Troller, to which I have already referred, calls our attention to this matter and has this to say:
We do not know what precautions our government is taking to assure that those who might claim historic rights do not develop beyond their present fishery, which we feel should be the maximum annual fishery they should be allowed, nor do we know if precautions are being taken to control such fisheries if a breakdown in our fisheries occurs, or if such foreign fisheries will be subjected to such restrictions as will be applicable to our nationals.
Then they go on to make certain recommendations with regard to historic fishing rights:
1.	That any recognition of historic rights the government may feel obligated to observe be confined to such species as have in the past been harvested by such claimants and further, that such parties be limited to their present annual harvest of those species, excepting wherein there may be an intermingling of anadromous types of fish to which another country contributes. In

Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones such instances, there should be equitable consideration for the fishing rights of that country for those species in the areas involved.
2.	That any recognition of historic rights should be subject to revision by Canada, for reasons of abuse of our fisheries and improper behaviour toward our fishermen.
3.	That no permanent recognition he given to historic rights prior to a trial period of some years in which to assess the effectiveness and further complications of an extended fishing limit.
In concluding this statement they say: Those who might claim historic rights offer nothing in return.
There we have one position. Another is that taken by the fishermen's union which, as I have already indicated, is that they are calling for the defeat of the measure unless it is amended to exclude all foreign fishermen from the 12 mile limit outside a base line which is clearly defined by legislation. This means, of course, complete and full operation of the restriction.
Again, as referred to in the discussion tonight, I believe, there are those who would subject the traditional fishing nations to a phasing out process whereby they would be given a certain length of time to change their pattern of fishing. I think this is a very important matter. I realize, of course, that discussions are still going on with those who have or claim to have traditional fishing rights. However, as has been pointed out by the fishermen's union, I would emphasize that there is no intention whatsoever to seek an amendment or change as far as the treaties are concerned under which some nations have historic fishing rights, and the union, of course, is taking very strong exception to that fact.
So I think this whole matter is one of great importance. We wish the minister well in all the discussions that are going on with other nations but we do urge him to seek in every possible way to assure the safeguarding of the rights of Canadian fishermen and the Canadian people as far as the fisheries of this nation are concerned.
There has been discussion tonight about the designation of the zones or the base lines. Again this is something to which great exception is taken by the united fishermen and allied workers union. They feel very strongly that this matter should not be left to the governor in council but should be included in the legislation. Once again I would refer to their statement, to which I have already referred twice, to point out that they say that the base lines should be clearly defined by legislation and net left to be defined or amended by secret orders in council. Apparently this is going to be done at some future date. We are not just sure when. I suppose it will be when the discussions currently being

carried on are completed. But, as has been noted tonight by other speakers, we have very little or no information upon which to base commendation or criticism of government intentions with respect to this particular matter. We are left completely in the dark and will have to trust to the discretion, wisdom and political diplomacy of the minister to arrive at the most satisfactory conclusions to these matters. I do not think this is altogether satisfactory to the fishermen. I do not think it is altogether satisfactory to us because we believe there should be something more clear and more definite upon which to base consideration of this particular measure.
We appreciate the fact that the bill is to be referred to the standing committee on marine and fisheries. Once again let me say that I believe that committee should have considered many of these factors long ago. The minister would then have had the benefit of the suggestions of the fishing industry, the fishermen's union and other interested individuals with the result that as he entered upon these negotiations and discussions he would have had a clear understanding of what these interested parties consider should be involved in the negotiation and discussion of these matters.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: LEGISLATION RESPECTING TERRITORIAL WATERS AND FISHERIES LAWS
speechtext:
You will perhaps have surmised, Mr. Speaker, that there are few subjects on which those of us from the Atlantic provinces, and who represent the people of those provinces by the sea, feel more deeply than the preservation of our fisheries.
In the four provinces there are some 32 constituencies, and of these 29 are touched intimately in their lives by the north Atlantic. Moreover, sir, discussion of the fisheries is not a new matter in this house. There was a time, sir, when fisheries rather than wheat was the staple of debate here; and in those days the debates were robust and lively, as the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) sought to remind us somewhat earlier this evening.
It is well to remember that fishing is, after all, our most historic industry. It is well to remember too that fishing is far more than an industry. To a very great extent it touches and shapes the lives of the people involved in it. Consequently, the demarcation of Canada's internal waters, the demarcation of her territorial sea, and the demarcation of her fishing zones are no mere assertion of a mature nationhood. Rather, this is an assertion that this country is not prepared to stand idly by, doing nothing, while the fisheries are being wantonly devastated.
That phrase, "wantonly devastated", is not perhaps perfectly exact, for the truth is that no Canadian fisherman and no fisherman from any foreign country is prepared to see the great north Atlantic fisheries wiped out either by design or by carelessness. The problem has been that no government has had established any conclusive jurisdiction over large areas of these seas. Of course the fact that the difficulties that have arisen have sprung largely from an absence of jurisdiction has been very little consolation to the people who saw the source of their livelihood ravaged, or to the scientists who were prepared to devote their time and energy to the preservation of this great natural resource.
Three things are necessary; first, the establishment of straight base lines; second, the establishment by clear reaffirmation of Canada's rights relative to certain waters such as the gulf of St. Lawrence and the bay of Fundy and, third, the fixing of the extent of Canada's fishing zones. I am pleased to see that the bill now before the house envisages provision for all these necessities.
It happens that the constituency which I have the honour to represent, by reason of its peculiar shape and location at the extremity of the mainland of Nova Scotia, is one in which all these three points have a direct application. Both the Northumberland strait
Business of the House
and St. George's bay are within the gulf of St. Lawrence. At the same time, the entire Guysborough shore, from Ecum Secum to Mulgrave, will be benefited greatly from the establishment of a Canadian fishing zone 12 miles wide drawn from a base line straight from cape to cape.
When this bill has been proclaimed Canada's fishing zone will extend nine miles beyond the present three mile limit. The function of this portion of the bill, as I understand it, is to establish the existence of Canadian fishing zones. Let me say here parenthetically, Mr. Speaker, that it is my understanding also that since these zones are shortly to be moved farther out to sea in many places-that is, just as soon as the straight base lines have been defined and published-these zones will not be enforced in their temporary locations. Then the bill authorizes the governor in council to establish the necessary straight base lines, these to be drawn from one major headland to another.
For example, in the case of the southern and eastern shores of Nova Scotia, I think what is envisaged is a series of lines beginning at cape Sable, touching the principal headlands and encompassing the larger offshore islands along to cape Canso and thence to Scatari island. When this base line has been settled all the waters landward of this line will be defined as internal waters of Canada. The territorial waters of Canada will be three miles of sea immediately seaward of this base line. The fishing zones of Canada will be the nine miles of sea immediately seaward of the territorial sea.
Generally, as provided by clause 4 of the bill, all fishing both within the internal waters of Canada and in the 12 miles between the base line and the limit of the fishing zone will be under the sole jurisdiction of the government of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it ten o'clock?

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion the Canada Council to the standing committee on public accounts, and resolution No. 18, to refer the public accounts volumes I, II and III, together with the Auditor General's reports thereon, to the standing committee on public accounts. I understand these will go through with no debate. Then we will go on with the estimates of the Department of External Affairs and on Monday, as mentioned by the Prime Minister, there will be a motion to go into supply.

subtopic: WESTVILLE,   N.S.,-PROPOSED REMOVAL OF STATION AGENT
WESTVILLE,   N.S.,-PROPOSED REMOVAL OF STATION AGENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday last I addressed a question to the Minister of Transport, which was as follows:
I should like to ask the Minister of Transport if he has received a telegram from the mayor of the town of Westville requesting his support in connection with the proposed removal of the Canadian National agent from the station in that community, thus placing it on a caretaker basis. If so, would the minister request the board of transport commissioners to postpone such action until the legislation standing on the order paper in the name of the minister is passed by this house?
I bring this matter to the attention of the house because I understand a telegram was sent by the mayor of this fine mining town in my constituency and a reply was sent by the minister stating that he would assist in the matter. A representative of the board of transport commissioners went to the area on April 21, I believe, and a hearing was held attended by many people, following which a letter was sent by the board of transport commissioners to the town clerk stating that the agent would be removed from this station if further submissions were not made within a 30 day period.
This is a most important matter for this mining town, one which has been a hard luck town for many years as a result of the closing of coal mines, which has led to a labour surplus not only in the town itself but in the whole constituency of Pictou. The history of this matter is well known in the district. The area served by the New Glasgow office is a designated area and to remove the agent from Westville station would be the last step before closing the station altogether. At the present time an application is being made by

the C.N.R. to remove the centre of the line which runs from Stellarton to Oxford Junction, that is, to remove the heart from a community which, though it may not be well known in this house, is well known in Nova Scotia-Tatamagouche to Scotsburn. This proposal to take out the middle of this line or, if I might put it more roughly, take out the guts of this line would, together with the closing of Westville station, be disastrous to the whole area. I believe the submissions put forward at the hearing held by this particular officer of the board of transport commissioners gave the reason why the traffic has been cut down so greatly, namely the removal of the Canadian National Express Agency to a private individual.
I am appealing to the minister because he has the responsibility of reporting for the Atlantic development board, a board which was set up to assist the Atlantic area. If there were no rail service it would be difficult to get new industries into the area, even with the help of the Department of Industry. As I stated, many people attended this hearing, including the provincial members Donald R. MacLeod and Harvey A. Veniot, representatives from the various municipalities in the area, officers of the department of trade and industry in Halifax, representatives of chambers of commerce, and merchants in the area as well as interested citizens. The principal brief was presented by Mayor Duggan, the mayor of this hard hit town.
I would ask the Minister of Transport, in accordance with the telegram, to request the board of transport commissioners to adjourn this matter so that rail services may still be provided for this area. If this were done, the Atlantic development board as well as the area development agency under the new Department of Industry would be given an opportunity to do something for this area.

subtopic: WESTVILLE,   N.S.,-PROPOSED REMOVAL OF STATION AGENT
speechtext:
In answer to the hon. member I can say it is a fact that on April 14 the minister received a telegram from the mayor of Westville which reads:
Board of railway commissioners are having a hearing here Tuesday re closing of Westville station we are objecting to same. Would appreciate your assistance to prevent this.
A day later, on April 15, the minister answered as follows:
Application of C.N.R. is being investigated by board of transport commissioners district inspector and report on investigation will be considered by board. Understand full opportunity will be given to municipal representatives to make representations to board's district inspector. I am referring your representations to the board of transport commissioners.
That is signed by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill). Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I

feel that the board of transport commissioners will take good care of this problem for the good of the citizens concerned.

URANIUM-DISPOSITION OF UNFILLED PORTION OF GUNNAR MINES CONTRACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a trade union member of 23 years standing I raise a question tonight on behalf of my fellow union members. The question I asked the minister the other day was: What is the government's intention with respect to the disposition of 1,200,000 pounds of uranium oxide from the Gunnar mines unfilled contract? I intended to put this supplementary question but was stopped in my tracks by Mr. Speaker and had to use the ruse of this evening's procedure in order to make my point: Is consideration being given to placing this contract with Metal Mines Limited, formerly known as Faraday Mines, in the Bancroft area, which is scheduled to close June 30 unless the contract is provided?
There was a brief submitted by the Bancroft and district workers local union 1006 of the international union of mine, mill and smelter workers to the Hon. Charles M. Drury, Minister of Industry, on May 19. In view of the shortness of my time, Mr. Speaker, I think I can most usefully use the time available by quoting from the brief, and I do urge the minister to give further consideration to their representations. I presume, from the gleam in the parliamentary secretary's eye, that he is intending to respond favourably to my representations later on. This brief reads:
The Bancroft and district workers local union 1006 of the international union of mine, mill and smelter workers (Canada), representing the employees of the Metal Mines Limited (Faraday Uranium Mines), Bancroft, Ontario, are making this representation with a view to preventing the closure of these mining operations. Their closure will work great hardships on many people, and create another depressed area in our nation.
The members of our union in Bancroft were both disappointed and alarmed when they heard the announcement made on May 4, 1964, that uranium delivery contracts would not be renewed by the government's crown corporation. These workers had hopefully anticipated, despite threats of closure, that the government would in the future interests of the nation continue the stockpiling of uranium.
This optimistic conclusion by the mine workers in Bancroft was a direct result of promises made to them during the previous federal election campaign.
I am sure the parliamentary secretary will refer to that. The brief continues:
In order to ensure that these promises would not be forgotten, our membership over the past period of time has continued to examine ways and means by which this small mining community could be saved from becoming a depressed area. In this, we have co-operated with the various community organizations, who we believe also have made proposals to the government. We believe the
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion proposals we are now making are workable and provide a proper solution to the problem facing our industry.
Then the brief goes on to make certain proposals. They propose that for immediate relief and to prevent the proposed closure of the Bancroft operations of Metal Mines Limited on June 30, the government should revert to these operations the unsold Gunnar Mines United Kingdom contract of 1,200,000 pounds of uranium oxide. They go on to deal with the possibilities of doing this and suggest a practical way in which it can be approached.
Then the next recommendation is:
2.	As a long range prospective to the problems facing the uranium industry, we again propose that the government institute some measures of stockpiling which will ensure that the three uranium communities are able to continue and that the industry will be competitive in the future.
Then they go on to say:
All engineering and political experts indicate that by 1970, there will be a large commercial demand for uranium oxide, arising from the development of uranium power and other commercial uses such as steel alloys. At that time, we repeat, it is important that the sources of supply be varied and monopoly control by one company be avoided.
I think that is a very good suggestion indeed. They conclude:
3.	New industry in Bancroft-One cannot look at the economic future of the Bancroft area without consideration of the development of a wider industrial base. It is important that even while the uranium industry operates, that secondary industries should be able to complement this basic industry to ensure the stability of employment over a long period of time. It is important, even if the uranium industry be assisted to continue and should function over the next few years, that at no time should the community be dependant upon this one industry alone.
I think that is a very constructive suggestion.
In conclusion, we wish to impress upon your government the urgency of the situation. It is now the middle of May. We are faced with the mine's closure on June 30. We have been given to understand from press reports that the question of Gunnar Mines undelivered contract is before the government. We have every hope that the government will be acting on this immediately and that this contract will be given to the Bancroft area. At the same time, we also urge that the long term viewpoint be considered and that through the use of some method of stockpiling and the establishment of secondary industry, the government will take steps to insure a diversified and competitive uranium industry in three stable and prosperous communities protected against the vagaries of one industry, through the establishment of secondary industries.
I have quoted briefly from the union's proposals, Mr. Speaker, and I do urge the government to give them consideration. I am sure that the hon. member who represents this area is very concerned about this matter; he asked a question about it on orders of the

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion day today and I hope to hear from him later. I see from looking at the parliamentary secretary that we can anticipate a favourable response to our representations.

maintopic: URANIUM-DISPOSITION OF UNFILLED PORTION OF GUNNAR MINES CONTRACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know from the oral question that the hon. member for Hastings-Frontenac (Mr. Webb) posed earlier today that he is vitally concerned with unemployment and its consequences in the Bancroft area. I also gather from the remarks of the hon. member for Kootenay West that he too is concerned about this matter. I can assure both hon. gentlemen that this matter is also very much in the mind of the Prime Minister. Our uranium mines are in difficulties. They are in difficulties in the Elliot Lake area as well as at Bancroft. No one could be more aware of this fact than the hon. member for Algoma East.
What, Mr. Speaker, can be done about it? The hon. member for Kootenay West asked about the undelivered portion of the Gunnar contract, involving some 1,200,000 pounds of
uranium oxide. If it is distributed among the remaining producers it could keep them all running for another two months, no more than that. The government is therefore considering an incentive program. The price of $4.19 a pound will not change, but the work will go to the producer who is willing to do the most stockpiling on the side. In other words, the one which is prepared, partly at its own expense, to create the most man-hours of employment will get the contract. Invitations to tender phrased along these lines will be going out over the week end.
There is, of course, the longer term problem. Every effort is being made by the Department of Industry, the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys and the Department of Labour to find alternative opportunities for the workers who are being laid off at Canada's uranium mines. These efforts are meeting with some success. Further announcements along these lines will be made at a later date.
